n: Given on Christmas Day 1832, during the “nullification crisis,” when South Carolina defied federal law. The Lord foretells wars beginning with a South Carolina rebellion. The Civil War began there at Fort Sumter in April 1861, more than 28 years later.

f.g: South Carolina was the first state to secede (December 1860), and the Civil War’s first shots were fired at Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor.

n: From that beginning, war would eventually spread to all nations.

f.w: war will be poured out upon all nations

n: The South would divide from the North and seek help from other nations, including Great Britain—which the Confederacy did attempt. Nations would then call on other nations, widening war worldwide.

f.g: The Confederacy sought British recognition and support during the Civil War.

n: Enslaved people would rise against their masters and be organized and trained for war. During the Civil War, many formerly enslaved men fought as soldiers.
The “remnants” left in the land—understood by Latter-day Saints as the descendants of Book of Mormon peoples—would rise up and greatly trouble the Gentiles.
Through war, famine, plague, earthquake, and storms, people everywhere will feel God’s chastening, until the decreed end comes to all nations as they now exist.

f.g: The complete ending that God has determined.

f.w: a full end of all nations

n: This will happen so that the cries of persecuted Saints and their shed blood no longer rise to the Lord asking for justice.

f.g: Hebrew for “Lord of Hosts”—Lord of armies.

n: The response for the Saints is not panic but faithfulness: stand in holy places and don’t be moved, for the Lord’s coming is near.
